item.title: Trey Songz Withdraws Promoter Lawsuit After Seeking Over $500K
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Trey Songz withdrew his lawsuit against Texas promoter Darryl Austin without prejudice, leaving the door open to refile.
item.content:encoded:
Trey Songz has withdrawn a lawsuit seeking more than $500,000 from a Texas promoter over a Fort Worth concert that never went ahead as planned.

The dismissal was filed “without prejudice,” according to MyNewsLA, leaving room for the dispute with Darryl Austin to return to court. The case was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court.

That type of dismissal allows a plaintiff to bring the same claims again, subject to filing deadlines. Those time limits keep running after a case is withdrawn.

Trey Songz Productions LLC brought the breach-of-contract case after a planned August 8 appearance at Will Rogers Auditorium fell apart.

AllHipHop covered the company’s demand in August, when the dispute centered on missed payments and the decision to move the show.

Under the deal finalized April 16, Austin was to pay a quarter of the performance fee the next day, another quarter on July 8 and the balance before the concert. The suit alleged the fee was fixed regardless of ticket sales.

The company said Austin paid the first installment but missed the second. He then sought a postponement, setting off a disagreement over both the money and whether the performance should go ahead.

Songz’s team said it had offered help with promotion and believed Austin had not done enough to sell the event. The singer’s side rejected the proposed delay and demanded the next payment under the agreement.

The lawsuit alleged that Austin still pushed the show to an undetermined date. Fans looking for tickets saw a postponement notice on Ticketmaster, while Songz’s side complained that the notice did not explain who made the decision.

The company sought damages for the unpaid performance fee, lost premium meet-and-greet income and harm to its reputation and future earning power. It also sought legal costs.

Austin challenged the California proceedings while representing himself. He described the concert fight as a “Texas-centered dispute” in a motion seeking to quash service of the summons.

Austin said he lived in Texas, had not visited California in about a decade and handled the negotiations by phone and email from Texas. His motion had been set for a November 19 hearing before Judge Phu Nguyen.

item.title: Skepta Questions Racial Double Standard For Aging Rappers
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Skepta questioned why Black rappers feel pushed out as they age while white rock stars keep performing into later life.
item.content:encoded:
Skepta questioned why Black rappers feel pressure to leave music as they get older while white rock stars keep their place onstage.

In an interview published November 6 by British GQ, the 44-year-old addressed the issue after its interviewer brought up André 3000’s concerns about rapping past 40.

He pointed to Iggy Pop performing shirtless as an older rock star. Skepta acknowledged questioning his own future, then decided, “bruv, I’m still making the best music.”

“Why can Iggy Pop grow old and still be on stage with his top off doing rock music, but we can’t? All of them, all the rock bands. [But] Black rappers get to 35, 38 and start panicking. So why is it okay for white people and not Black people to grow old in music? This is something Black artists need to stop doing to themselves,” Skepta said.

His condition was that his lyrics should fit his life now. He also urged older Black artists to keep contributing to the culture.

“The stuff we’ve got is a blessing, and the kids need more people who are speaking up for the culture, to stay in the culture and carry the work on,” the legendary rapper said.

The interview accompanied his new album, The Fork and Knife.

André discussed his difficulty writing raps during the 2023 rollout for New Blue Sun. He told GQ, “I’m 48 years old. And not to say that age is a thing that dictates what you rap about, but in a way it does.”

He had kept working with producers and trying to write. In a separate NPR conversation, he explained that playing the flute felt immediate and free, while writing lyrics had become harder. He wanted listeners to know New Blue Sun had no rapping before they bought it and left open a return to rap.

His solo catalog has since expanded to include Moving Day and 7 Piano Sketches. The latter consists of solo piano recordings, some begun almost a decade earlier during a stay in Texas with his son.

Más Tiempo was launched in 2023 with fellow grime artist Jammer. Skepta’s wider career also includes the fashion label MAINS and the Mercury Prize-winning 2016 album Konnichiwa.

Skepta has also spent this year building a musical life beyond the sound that made him famous. His Más Tiempo project held its first Hï Ibiza residency from May 2 through October 3, with Saturday shows in the venue’s Club Room.

Black Coffee occupied the Theatre during the same Saturday residency season. The run followed Skepta’s 2025 appearance at Carl Cox’s Sunday residency at [UNVRS], extending his move into house music and DJing.

item.title: Jamie Foxx’s Halloween Festival Draws Police After Reported Stabbing
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jamie Foxx's SKVLK Fest drew deputies after a reported stabbing at his mansion, a year after the GloRilla bottle incident.
item.content:encoded:
Jamie Foxx‘s annual Halloween festival drew a police response Saturday (November 7) after a guest was reportedly stabbed at his Thousand Oaks, California mansion.

A Ventura County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson told the Daily Mail that deputies responded “for a party call” and “there was a juvenile arrested.”

TMZ reported a guest’s neck wound was treated there and a suspect was arrested on suspicion of assault with a deadly weapon.

The gathering was SKVLK Fest, the Halloween event Foxx hosts with his daughter Anelise. Images and video described in the reporting showed people in handcuffs as hundreds of costumed guests were told to leave.

A sign at the event read “No Real or Fake Weapons,” according to a photograph. Foxx’s presence when the incident occurred was unclear.

The party also featured Hip-Hop performances. Foxx shared posts highlighting Offset, DJ Stevie J and OhGeesy, while praising Anelise for organizing the night.

The available reports did not establish what led to the confrontation.

This year’s event had been moved from October 31 because of rain. The festival combines live music with carnival rides and costumes, and its official performer archive lists GloRilla, Sexyy Red, Tyga and Ty Dolla $ign among past guests.

It was the second consecutive year that trouble at the family’s Halloween gathering drew attention.

In October 2025, someone threw a bottle toward GloRilla while she performed at SKVLK Fest.

Foxx took the microphone and confronted the crowd after her set was interrupted. The 2025 party was an invite-only gathering for teens and young adults at the same Southern California property.

“Why would you throw something at the stage, man? Why? This is for free!” he said during that incident.

He questioned why a guest would behave that way in his home, briefly threatened to close the party and then encouraged GloRilla to keep performing once order was restored.

“You throw some shit in my house?” Foxx asked.

The latest incident came days after Foxx welcomed his third child, his first with girlfriend Alyce Huckstepp. The couple’s baby news followed a pregnancy announcement in May. Anelise is his younger daughter; he is also father to Corinne Foxx.

item.title: Blacc Sam Credits Jay-Z With Helping Secure Marathon’s Live Nation Partnership
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Blacc Sam detailed how Jay-Z and Roc Nation helped Marathon Clothing secure order fulfillment, legal support and a Live Nation advance.
item.content:encoded:
Blacc Sam credited Jay-Z and Roc Nation with helping The Marathon Clothing handle a flood of orders after Nipsey Hussle’s death, leading to a Live Nation partnership that supplied an advance and legal support.

Speaking on One54 Africa alongside his father, Dawit Asghedom, Sam explained how the family protected Nipsey’s business as it grew suddenly. Nipsey was killed outside his Marathon Clothing store in Los Angeles on March 31, 2019.

“Jay-Z and Roc Nation came in early and helped us with a partnership with Live Nation to clean up our website because we had so many orders that we didn’t even have a way to ship out or produce,” Sam said.

He recalled an offer to address the immediate backlog before settling on a business agreement.

“We’re gonna produce everything. We’re gonna fulfill the orders so your website doesn’t get shut down,” Sam recalled being told. “And if there’s a deal to do, we could do a deal. If not, it’s on the strength.”

Jay-Z’s support for Nipsey stretched back years. In 2013, he bought 100 copies of the rapper’s $100 mixtape Crenshaw, putting $10,000 behind the independent artist’s direct-to-fan sales campaign.

Sam said the later help went beyond clearing unfilled purchases. “So Live Nation came in and treated us like family,” he said.

“They entered into a partnership with us and gave us a big advance, and they took over all the merchandise,” Sam continued.

He said access to that infrastructure included lawyers who pursued counterfeit products and websites using Nipsey’s intellectual property or the Marathon name.

“Any fake websites that were up, any bootlegs that were out, they were sending cease and desists and sending lawyers,” he said.

Sam also described a separate fight involving attempts to claim the Marathon name through a corporation. He said lawyers connected to the Cochran firm helped the family challenge that effort.

Sam did not identify who he suspected was behind it, but AllHipHop.com reported that the Crips were the ones trying to hijack the name through a company, Crips LLC.

He said the other side backed away as the proceedings moved toward identifying who ran the company. His account placed that dispute alongside the broader work of protecting the brand after Nipsey’s death.

For the Live Nation agreement, Sam described an eventual move back toward operating independently after the advance was recouped. He did not give a dollar amount for the advance in the clip.

“We were able to recoup the, the advance they gave us, and we were able to kinda pivot off on our own,” he said.

The family’s business work has continued across music, clothing and restaurants. Marathon Burger added a Terminal 1 location at LAX in October, extending the food business beyond its neighborhood storefronts.

Sam credited the support network Nipsey built with helping the family carry that work forward.

“Everything was honestly based on the relationships, um, that people had with my brother and how mu- how much they loved bro,” he said.

item.title: T-Pain Turns His DJ & Wife’s Search For A Third Partner Into Reality Series
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: T-Pain's new Nappy Boy Network series follows DJ Montay and Shonte Renee as they seek a third partner, with a November 11 debut.
item.content:encoded:
T-Pain is putting his longtime DJ’s relationship at the center of a new dating series as he expands Nappy Boy into reality television.

He created and executive produced “Searching For A Third,” which follows DJ Montay and his wife, Shonte Renee, as they look for another woman to join their relationship. The first two episodes arrive November 11 at 8 P.M. Eastern on Nappy Boy Network’s YouTube channel.

The series announcement describes a search involving first meetings, chemistry, jealousy and the boundaries of an existing partnership.

“My favorite thing about this show is that it’s real,” said T-Pain. “Montay has been like a brother to me for many years, so getting to support him and Shonte on their quest for love was both special and entertaining as hell.”

The connection is personal. Montay has spent years working alongside the singer as a DJ and musical collaborator.

The new series adds a television project to a business that already reaches beyond recording. Nappy Boy has operated in entertainment and gaming, and T-Pain has built an audience on Twitch through livestreams that put his personality alongside his music.

He also bought a 50,000-square-foot Tallahassee warehouse to bring his growing operations together. That physical investment gave the different parts of the company a shared home as he built businesses around the Nappy Boy name.

Paperwork for a broader media business predated this week’s announcement. Nappy Boy Entertainment filed an application for the Nappy Boy Network name in April.

The goods and services listed in that application included film and television production, podcasts, video distribution and online reality programming, alongside clothing and downloadable entertainment.

That range connects the new show to an existing effort to bring several kinds of entertainment under one brand. T-Pain’s automotive venture has also paired his music with his interest in drifting through a partnership with HertLife.

The season will follow a group of women interested in joining the couple.

For this series, Montay and Renee will have to find someone who fits both of them while working through the conversations and compromises that come with expanding their relationship.

Episodes will continue weekly after the November 11 launch, with a two-part reunion planned for early next year.

item.title: ISINA Is Building a New Home for Independent Artists to Connect, Create, and Be Discovered
item.dc:creator: Brxton Lee
item.description: ISINA connects emerging artists with collaborators, industry professionals, and fans to help grow their careers.
item.content:encoded:
The artist-focused platform brings together emerging musicians, music industry professionals, and fans to create meaningful opportunities for collaboration, discovery, and career development.

LOS ANGELES, CA — [November 6, 2026] — While the music industry seems easier than ever to enter, the challenge has shifted to helping artists get seen in a fast-changing landscape. Rising company ISINA, an AI artist discovery platform built by artists, aims to empower artists at every stage of their career. The global music and social platform has brought together musicians, producers, songwriters, industry professionals, and fans to transform music discovery, relationship building, and artist/audience development. Artists who use the platform to its fullest potential can share tracks, showcase their skills, and connect with potential collaborators.

A Platform Designed for Artists, by Artists

ISINA lets musicians create unique artist profiles, share original music, and highlight their skills while connecting with potential collaborators, fans, and industry professionals. Beyond discovery, ISINA leverages its established network of culture-shifting creative professionals, including multi-Grammy Award-winning songwriter and producer Walter Afanasieff, acclaimed recording artist and producer Robin Thicke, and legendary musician and arranger Greg Phillinganes, among others, to help artists reach the next level. 

Through its talent search and artist development initiatives, ISINA offers select emerging artists professional guidance, collaboration with experienced music creators, and career advancement.

More Than Music Discovery: Building a Community

At its core, ISINA recognizes that sustainable careers are built through more than streams, followers, and viral moments. They are built through relationships. For independent musicians navigating an increasingly competitive industry, ISINA offers a centralized destination to showcase their work, expand their networks, and pursue new creative and professional opportunities.

“Every artist deserves the opportunity to have their music heard, connect with people who believe in their talent, and build something meaningful around their creativity,” said Alexey Kurochkin, Founder. “We’re building ISINA to be more than a place to upload music. We want it to be a community where artists can find their people, develop their craft, and discover opportunities that can help move their careers forward.” 

Turning Discovery Into Real Opportunities

ISINA’s artist development initiatives have already helped emerging musicians take meaningful steps in their careers. Artists including Took4Granted and Shannon Jae Prior have been featured among the platform’s development success stories, while singer Cooper Phillip collaborated with ISINA co-founder Walter Afanasieff on original music.

These examples reflect ISINA’s broader mission: to create a more direct connection between emerging talent and the people, resources, and opportunities that can support their professional growth. Whether an artist is releasing their first song, searching for a producer, building a fanbase, or taking the next step in their career, ISINA helps turn creative ambition into tangible progress.

Artists, music professionals, and fans can learn more and join the community by visiting www.isina.com.

⸻

About ISINA

ISINA is a global music discovery, networking, and artist development platform connecting emerging musicians, established industry professionals, and music fans. Founded with a mission to make music industry opportunities more accessible, ISINA provides artists with tools to showcase their talent, share original music, build their fanbases, connect with collaborators, and participate in talent discovery and development initiatives. Through its growing community and network of music industry professionals, ISINA is working to create meaningful opportunities for the next generation of artists.

For more information, visit www.isina.com.

item.title: Big Daddy Kane To Enter Berklee Hip-Hop Hall Of Fame
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Big Daddy Kane will enter Berklee's Hip-Hop Hall of Fame during a student-led ceremony and concert in Boston on November 19.
item.content:encoded:
Big Daddy Kane will enter Berklee College of Music’s Hip-Hop Hall of Fame during a ceremony and concert in Boston later this month.

Berklee announced that the Brooklyn MC will be inducted Thursday, November 19, at 8 P.M. inside the Berklee Performance Center.

The event will combine the formal honor with student performances, original work and new arrangements built around Kane’s catalog. Kane is also scheduled to perform a showcase set.

The induction places one of Hip-Hop’s sharpest technicians inside an institution designed to recognize artists, educators and culture bearers whose work helped build the genre.

Kane’s late-1980s run established him as a commanding lyricist and performer, with Long Live the Kane and It’s a Big Daddy Thing becoming foundational albums for generations of MCs.

His influence reaches beyond records. Kane helped set a new standard for breath control, stage movement, tailored style and romantic confidence at a time when rap performance was still defining its rules.

Songs such as “Ain’t No Half-Steppin'” and “Smooth Operator” remain central to his catalog, while his live show has kept that material active for audiences born long after its release.

Emmett G. Price III, dean of Berklee’s Africana Studies Division, said Kane “exemplifies this legacy, reflecting both the cultural significance and enduring influence of Hip-Hop.”

“For more than five decades, Hip-Hop has shaped cultures, inspired generations, and left an indelible mark on communities across the globe,” Price said. “This year, as in years past, we honor Hip-Hop’s past, celebrate its present, and embrace its future as a testament to Afrodiasporic brilliance, resilience, and hope.”

The Hall of Fame is part of Berklee’s broader Africana Studies work, which is marking its fifth anniversary. Previous inductees include Rakim, Roxanne Shante, Kid ‘n Play, Edo G, the Floor Lords, Barbara Thomas, the Wonder Twins and Berklee professor Prince Charles Alexander.

That list gives the program a wide view of Hip-Hop history. It honors star MCs alongside dancers, local builders and educators.

Kane’s induction adds a performer whose career connects Brooklyn’s late-1980s breakthrough to the modern classroom, where students study the writing, production and stagecraft that turned the music into a global culture.

Kane’s honor arrives as he also looks ahead creatively.

In a recent AllHipHop interview, he discussed plans for Curtain Call, the album he intends to make his final solo statement. He described a 10-song project that mirrors his debut while addressing adulthood, family and aging inside Hip-Hop.

The Berklee ceremony gives Kane another setting to connect that history with younger artists. Students will interpret the music that shaped his legacy before the veteran rapper takes the stage for his own performance on November 19.

item.title: Wale Brings Black Sports Leaders Into Gifted Week Career Program
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Wale's third Gifted Week includes Black sports industry leaders, a Howard University workshop and youth activities in Washington.
item.content:encoded:
Wale is bringing Black sports executives, agents and industry leaders into his third annual Gifted Week, with a Washington, D.C., panel focused on helping people build careers beyond the playing field.

The rapper and his management company, EQT, will hold the community program November 17-20. The organizers’ event listings include a Howard University workshop, a Washington Commanders flag football clinic and a sneaker and jersey design workshop.

The November 19 “Beyond the Field and Court” panel pairs Diverse Representation with the Washington Nationals. It will give attendees a chance to hear how Black professionals entered the sports business and developed their careers, with a networking reception also planned.

The panel is listed at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library.

A November 18 workshop at Howard University will bring together six executives working across sports and music for a film panel. The program invites participants to bring ideas and meet other people pursuing creative work.

That focus extends to the November 20 design workshop, where participants will work on sneaker and cleat concepts. The listings offer free registration, subject to approval and available space.

Gifted Week grew out of Wale’s effort to connect the next generation of artists and athletes in the region that raised him.

Its 2024 edition included a Nike sneaker design workshop, a Commanders youth football clinic, a poetry jam and open mic, plus a panel exploring the relationship between music and sports. That program ran alongside his Every Blue Moon Tour homecoming show at MGM National Harbor.

The celebration followed his 2023 Kennedy Center concert marking the 10th anniversary of The Gifted. Mayor Muriel Bowser designated November 10 as Wale Day in Washington.

Footwear has remained part of his business work. In October, Wale became a co-owner and chief creative officer of CapSole, a sneaker preservation company.

His role covers creative direction, cultural partnerships and growth. He also helped introduce Nike’s G.T. Future with basketball prospect AJ Dybantsa during NBA All-Star Weekend in 2025.

For the upcoming workshops, organizers will send exact locations to confirmed guests. The Commanders clinic’s registration page currently lists the event as full and offers a waitlist.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Legal War Explodes Over Naz Reid’s Cyborg Jesus Pendant
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Alex Moss New York sued jeweler Leo Khusro over alleged copies of the Cyborg Jesus pendant it first created for NBA star Naz Reid.
item.content:encoded:
Alex Moss’s jewelry company took its Cyborg Jesus pendant dispute to federal court, accusing a Houston jeweler of copying a design it first made for NBA player Naz Reid.

AMNY Global Inc., which does business as Alex Moss New York, filed the copyright lawsuit in Manhattan federal court. The defendant is Arsh Khusro, also known as Leo Khusro, who operates as leokhusro.

Moss is the company’s founder and designer. The complaint lists Drake, Tyler, the Creator, A$AP Rocky and Chief Keef among its clients.

The business sells custom pieces and jewelry collections through its website, a Mercer Street flagship store and luxury stockists.

The complaint identifies the disputed work as the Cyborg Robot Jesus Pendant and cites copyright registration VA 2-468-075. AMNY said it first created the piece for Reid, then offered it through its website and promoted it on Instagram.

AMNY accused Khusro of marketing products bearing its work or “designs that are substantially similar thereto.” It pointed to promotions on the @leokhusro Instagram account and alleged that several posts tagged Manhattan as their location.

“No one other than Plaintiff is authorized to manufacture, import, export, advertise, offer for sale or sell any goods utilizing the Cyborg Robot Jesus Work without the express permission of Plaintiff,” the company stated.

The filing includes a side-by-side comparison of photographs to support AMNY’s copying claim. The company also alleged that Khusro knew it owned the design and used it to benefit from the brand’s reputation.

“Defendant has been engaging in the illegal and infringing actions, as alleged herein, knowingly and intentionally, or with reckless disregard or willful blindness to Plaintiff’s rights, or in bad faith, for the purpose of trading on the reputation of Plaintiff and the Cyborg Robot Jesus Work,” the complaint alleged.

The design is part of Moss’s take on the Jesus piece, a staple of Hip-Hop jewelry. His futuristic versions have also been known as Cyborg Savior.

AMNY requested a jury trial. It sought its losses and Khusro’s profits or statutory damages, along with legal fees. The company also asked the court to stop the manufacture, promotion and sale of the accused products.

Its requests extended to a recall of allegedly infringing goods from distributors and retailers for destruction. AMNY sought an accounting of the money generated by the products and an asset freeze or trust over proceeds it claimed belonged to the company.

Judge Lorna G. Schofield set an initial conference for December 22 at 3:30 P.M. in Manhattan. Materials for that conference are due December 15.

item.title: Mike Tyson & Ric Flair Keep $50M Cannabis Lawsuit Alive
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Mike Tyson and Ric Flair can continue their $50 million cannabis fraud lawsuit after a federal judge rejected a dismissal bid.
item.content:encoded:
Mike Tyson and Ric Flair can keep pursuing their $50 million cannabis fraud lawsuit after a federal judge rejected an effort to throw out the case against five former business associates.

The ruling allows their federal racketeering claims to move forward, TMZ Sports reported. The defendants, Chad Bronstein, Adam Wilks, Nicole Cosby, James Case and Christopher Volo, have all denied wrongdoing in the dispute over Carma HoldCo and the cannabis businesses tied to the two stars.

Tyson and Flair filed the lawsuit in December 2025, accusing former Carma leaders and associates of enriching themselves through company money and deals made without approval. Carma, hemp company LGNDS LLC and Tyson 2.0 are also plaintiffs in the case, which is pending in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.

Carma’s business included the Tyson 2.0 and Ric Flair Drip brands, giving the company two famous names from boxing and wrestling to market its cannabis products. The lawsuit alleged that former executives used more than $1 million in company funds for personal expenses, including private jets, yacht costs and home renovations.

The plaintiffs also accused former executives of arranging unauthorized licensing deals and collecting hidden kickbacks. One alleged arrangement involved vape manufacturer DomPen, which the lawsuit claimed received access to Carma’s intellectual property through a deal that benefited Wilks.

Other allegations concern no-show jobs and efforts to inflate Carma’s value on paper. The plaintiffs brought those claims under the federal Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, arguing that the transactions were connected parts of a scheme inside the business.

The five defendants filed their joint dismissal motion in May after the plaintiffs revised the lawsuit. They argued that the second amended complaint failed to state a valid claim and asked the court to end the case before it went further.

AllHipHop covered the dispute when it first became public, including the defendants’ rejection of the allegations. Tyson and Flair sought a jury trial and more than $50 million in damages and legal fees.

“The Court’s decision allows the litigation to move forward, and we welcome that opportunity,” a Tyson 2.0 representative said.
